newsitem.title: USA: U.N. envoy to meet Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy to meet Mobutu.

text.p: U.N. envoy Raymond Chretien said on Monday he would meet ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko on the French Riviera on Wednesday and believed the international community is committed to fast action on the Zaire-Rwanda crisis.

He also said there were "various scenarios, various options" about how to get humanitarian aid to 1.1 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees set on the move by the crisis but sidestepped whether Canadian, American or other foreign forces might be used to accomplish this task.
Chretien, who is also Canada's ambassador to Washington, spoke at a news conference after pre-trip talks with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and other officials.
A former ambassador to Zaire, he is on a one-month mission to try to nail down a cease-fire in eastern Zaire as well as to plan for an international conference in the region.
At the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States was reviewing proposals for a multi-national force to guarantee distribution of relief aid to refugees.
"In the case of the French, we have received some ideas from the French in the last 24 hours. We're looking at them," Burns told a news briefing.
"But frankly, we need to know a lot more information from the French government about what it has in mind before we can possibly react to these ideas," he said.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said: "What we're proposing is that the international community -- Europe, the United States, African states -- organize so that there is a security force on the ground to guarantee people's safety."

Some U.S. officials said it would be hard for Washington to refuse to participate, given its push for an all-Africa crisis response force that could handle such crises in the future. But the Pentagon was said to be cool to a U.S. role in Zaire.
Chretien, named by U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros- Ghali last week, plans to leave for Nice early on Tuesday.
He would meet Mobutu, who is resting at his Mediterranean villa after cancer treatment in Switzerland, on Wednesday, then fly to Kinshasa to see Zaire's Prime Minister Kengo Wa Dondo.
He also asked to meet Tutsi rebels fighting Zaire's army on the border with Rwanda but that has not been arranged yet.
"I'm pleasantly surprised that there seems to be a great deal of political will (in the international community) to work very fast on the first part of my mandate," he said.

Chretien told reporters if the situation on the Zaire-Rwanda border remains calm for a few days, the humanitarian effort could move very quickly. But Rwanda must permit access to border airports, he said.
The first part of his three-part mandate involves developing urgent plans to defuse the crisis, establishing a cease-fire and a negotiating process.
A cease-fire announced by Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire on Monday seemed to be holding after a two-week offensive uprooted a million refugees with little food or water.
There was no immediate official Zairean comment on the cease-fire offer.

But Zaire reiterated its rejection of talks "while part of its territory is occupied by the aggressor," state radio said, referring to Rwanda, which is accused by Zaire of backing Tutsi rebels battling its army.
Chretien said he would discuss these issues with Mobutu.
Burns said U.S. special negotiator Howard Wolpe would be in Nairobi on Tuesday for a conference called by Kenya to focus on a humanitarian response to the Zaire crisis.

In addition, the special U.S. Rwanda-Burundi coordinator Richard Begosian was to leave Washington on Monday for talks in Zaire and Rwanda and a U.S. team was sent to Geneva to work with the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees on what Washington could do on the refugee question.

The United States has made available $30 million to the UNHCR for relief funding, in addition to $875 million contributed over the last two years for humanitarian programs in central Africa, Burns said.
